source.title: Precise Asymptotic Analysis of Deep Random Feature Models
source.authors: David Bosch; Ashkan Panahi; B. Hassibi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present. The plotted curves are not available as readable values in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps model width and reports training and generalization error for random-feature regression models, conceptually testing size-wise risk behavior with a different model and experimental setup.
record.gate_note: The paper varies n/p and plots training and generalization error for one- and two-layer random-feature models under ℓ₂ and elastic-net regularization (Figures 1–2). The text explicitly says the two-layer model has lower generalization error than the one-layer model across the tested n/p values, but does not describe a fall-rise-fall curve or its relation to interpolation. The plotted values cannot be read from the supplied text. Double-descent results cited from other work are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper proving universality and exact asymptotics for deep random-feature regression. Double descent appears only through citations (refs 6–9, 37), and the authors draw no conclusion about it. Figures 1–2 plot generalization error against the width ratio γ = p/n under ℓ₂ and elastic-net regularization. The prose never describes the curves' shape, a peak, or an interpolation threshold, and the plotted values are not readable in the text. The only stated result is that the 2-layer model has lower generalization error than the 1-layer model. No version can be judged from the study's own reported results.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with one correction. The authors prove that deep random-feature models are asymptotically equivalent to a layer-wise moment-matched Gaussian model and derive exact CGMT expressions for training and generalization error. They conclude that depth affects both errors, shown both experimentally and through the covariance eigendistribution. The experiments vary p/n, not n/p. They state no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use tanh random-feature regression, varying n/p at fixed n/d=1.5, and compare one- and two-layer models with ℓ₂ or elastic-net regularization; this is not the original deep-network size-sweep setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies layer depth and regularization type and strength; it reports lower generalization error for the two-layer model across tested n/p values.

fits_no_version.finding: Across all tested p/n values and both regularizers, the 2-layer random-feature model has lower generalization error than the 1-layer model. It has lower training error only at large regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding an untrained random-feature layer lowers ridge or elastic-net generalization error relative to a 1-layer random-feature model.

record.problems: The supplied text provides no readable numerical values for the plotted curves, and the authors do not describe their shape in prose. The experimental section does not state the absolute sample or model dimensions, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: There are no deep networks trained end to end, and the shape of test error against size is not reported.
There is no sample-count sweep near the threshold; n/d is fixed at 1.5.
The width sweep exists, but the text does not report whether the curve has a second descent past interpolation.
No effective-complexity predictor of the peak is tested.
Regularization strength is varied, but whether the peak appears or vanishes is not reported. Noise and multiple peaks are not studied.
There is no re-parameterisation by an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'n/p' misreads the figure axis γ = p/n. In the 1-layer case the authors call this ratio the measure of under- or overparameterization. The λ=10⁻⁵ curves could show an interpolation peak, but no value or prose describing one is available, so no verdict is possible. Figure 3 (eigendistribution against hidden width) does not bear on test error.

versions.untested_parts: The paper sweeps width for a two-layer deep random-feature model, but does not establish whether test error falls, peaks near the training-fit threshold, and falls again; it does not identify that threshold.
Training epochs or time are not varied.
The paper does not isolate increasing training-sample count near an interpolation threshold; n/p is varied while n/d is fixed at 1.5.
The width sweep includes random-feature model classes, but the supplied text does not establish a second descent past an interpolation point or a general curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The experiments do not test whether noise or variance drives a peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes one.
The paper does not re-express the curve using an effective number of parameters or test whether that produces an ordinary U-shape.
